content.jointProblem: Can Serbian-specific lemmatization, within-token script normalization and paradigm-aware retrieval reduce LinguaBot’s support-search misses toward its below-5% target while supporting vocabulary updates without full re-indexing? The first experiment would compare these components against the current Elasticsearch baseline on held-out support queries, explicitly testing transfer from reference and social-media corpora to banking and telecom terminology, mixed-script typos, retrieval precision and update costs.

rationale.text: Nikolić’s work directly addresses Serbian lemmatization across Latin and Cyrillic scripts, providing a relevant candidate component rather than evidence of validated support-search performance.

sources.quote: The proposed system handles both scripts transparently by applying a unified internal representation before lemmatization, then restoring the original script in the output.

rationale.text: Her retrieval research compares the principal alternatives relevant to LinguaBot’s morphological mismatch problem, including paradigm-aware indexing.

sources.quote: The paper evaluates three mitigation strategies — stemming, full lemmatization, and paradigm-based query expansion — comparing their precision and recall
Full lemmatization combined with paradigm-aware indexing yields the highest F1 score.

rationale.text: Her cross-script tokenization work specifically addresses script boundaries inside tokens, closely matching the company’s mixed-script typo problem.

sources.quote: We introduce a cross-script tokeniser that identifies script boundaries within tokens and normalises them before downstream processing

rationale.text: Her corpus-driven paradigm induction offers a candidate workflow for expanding morphological coverage as product vocabulary changes.

sources.quote: candidate lemmas are identified through lemmatisation, and their full inflectional paradigms are hypothesised by a rule engine and then validated against corpus evidence.

rationale.text: Her spelling-variation research provides evidence for comparing conservative normalization with methods intended to generalize to unfamiliar borrowings.

sources.quote: The lookup-table approach achieves the highest precision while the neural model generalises better to unseen foreign borrowings.

constraints.text: The solution must handle Serbian-specific inflection and automatic Latin–Cyrillic normalization, including script changes within words; replacing the stemmer alone would not cover the stated task.

sources.quote: our users freely switch between Latin and Cyrillic script mid-sentence — sometimes mid-word in typos.
Our current Elasticsearch setup uses a basic stemmer that was built for Croatian and misses a significant share of Serbian-specific forms.

constraints.text: The approach must integrate with the existing Elasticsearch search system and support new vocabulary without a full re-index or an expanding manual synonym-maintenance burden.

sources.quote: Our current Elasticsearch setup uses a basic stemmer
maintaining those lists manually does not scale as clients add new product terminology every quarter.
can be updated when new vocabulary arrives without a full re-index.

constraints.text: Evaluation must connect to the measured no-useful-result problem and the company’s below-5% target, using the available labelled pairs and linguist validation; that target is not an established outcome.

sources.quote: in a sample of 12,000 real support queries from one bank client, about 18% returned no useful result
We have a labelled query-response dataset of around 85,000 pairs across all clients
our two in-house linguists can annotate or validate proposed solutions.
A good outcome is getting that 18% miss rate below 5% and keeping it there with a manageable maintenance process.

constraints.text: Scope tooling and data work to approximately EUR 8,000 and produce something testable within six months; this does not establish a budget for researcher time.

sources.quote: Budget for tooling or data work is modest — around 8,000 EUR — and we want something testable within six months.

risks: Transfer remains unvalidated: corpus lemmatization accuracy, social-media tokenization performance and retrieval-test-collection results do not establish performance on LinguaBot’s banking and telecom support queries. The first experiment must measure these gaps explicitly.
New product names and borrowings may receive incorrect paradigms: the morphological lexicon study reports 78.6% paradigm correctness for borrowings, below its result for common vocabulary.
Normalization and query expansion may merge distinct terms or increase irrelevant matches. Lowering the no-result rate without checking answer relevance could conceal a precision regression.
More than half of the observed misses were attributed to morphology or script confusion, but the evidence does not establish that fixing these causes alone can reach the below-5% target.
The published methods do not demonstrate vocabulary updates without full Elasticsearch re-indexing. Existing index design may limit which approaches satisfy this requirement.
Researcher availability and committed company engineering and annotation time are unknown. A six-month joint project needs explicit staffing and funding agreement.
Permission to share client queries, required de-identification, deployment restrictions, compute availability and exact commercial-use licence terms remain unknown.
questions: What time can Nikolić commit over the next six months, and who will own implementation, linguistic validation and ongoing maintenance at LinguaBot?
Does the EUR 8,000 cover only tooling and data work, and what separate funding is available for researcher and engineering time?
Can the researcher access the 85,000 labelled pairs and the 12,000-query failure sample? What client approvals, de-identification and secure-access arrangements are required?

How is 'no useful result' defined, and do the labels identify relevant knowledge-base documents as well as responses? Can the first experiment use client- and time-separated held-out queries with separate morphology, mixed-script and new-vocabulary slices?
What relevance, latency and maintenance-cost limits must accompany the below-5% miss-rate target, and is that target intended for the original bank sample or all clients?

What Elasticsearch version, analyzers, mappings and update mechanisms are deployed? Does 'without a full re-index' permit targeted document updates, query-time expansion or versioned external dictionaries?
Which published tools and datasets are currently available, and do their exact licences permit the intended commercial deployment? What compute and external-service restrictions apply?
Can the first experiment include a simulated quarterly vocabulary update to test unseen-term coverage, correction effort and whether the no-full-re-index requirement is achievable?
